metadata.title: Taxel Atlas hardware
metadata.scope: Tactile gloves, tactile robot hands and add-on touch sensors for dexterous manipulation data, and the hand-tracking gloves catalog datasets paired with them. Each device lists the catalog datasets recorded with it.
metadata.license: CC BY 4.0 (text and data); photos belong to their makers

hardware.name: TachinGlove
hardware.taxels_note: per glove (TouchScale paper); the quick-release TachinGloveSnap variant has 783
specs: 880 taxels of 1.5 x 1.5 mm on the palmar side of the five fingers and palm (15 regions); spatial resolution below 2 mm
Range 0.2-30 N/cm^2, resolution 0.05 N/cm^2 (TouchScale paper); vendor lists normal and tangential force
Acquisition module on the back of the hand; 50 Hz over WiFi, 100 Hz over USB Type-C; external battery/power module
Vendor describes it as an intrinsically stretchable e-skin; 75 g per glove (launch press)
Snap variant (Sept 2026): detachable acquisition module, 783 sensing points, about 50 g
unconfirmed: The TouchScale paper names only the 'Tachin Glove'; the maker is identified from Chinese press and the vendor site (途见科技 / Tachin Technology Co., Ltd., tachin.com), which sells a 'TachinGlove' flexible tactile data glove under its EI-G series.

Availability: the vendor home page says 'Now Released, Global Pre-orders Now Open'; the Beijing launch event was 2026-08-20 and Pro/Lite versions were announced for October 2026. No public price. Classed commercial because the glove was already used for the 500 h TouchScale collection (data captured by Noitom).

Transduction principle not stated by the paper or vendor (paper: normal pressure; vendor: normal + tangential, 'intrinsically stretchable e-skin'; press traces the technology to Zhenan Bao's Stanford lab).
Battery: paper says >10 h; launch press says up to 6 h per charge (may differ by version).

Image is the vendor's marketing render from the home-page hero (3840x2160, 3.7 MB), not a plain product photo; a clean schematic is TouchScale Fig. 9 (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.10288v2/tactile_glove_config.png).
year=2026 from the earliest launch report found (June 2026).
vendor homepage says 'Now Released' and 'Global Pre-orders Now Open'; international shipping status not confirmed
press gives other counts (815 units, 'about a thousand'); the 783 here is from the English datasheet
'Pro'/'Lite' variant names could not be verified; press mentions a quick-release 'TachinGlove Snap'
TouchScale's 'Tachin glove' (880 taxels, same 1.5 mm cells and 50/100 Hz) is likely an earlier version of this product (catalog notes, not vendor-stated)
image is a marketing render (handshake) from the vendor homepage

hardware.name: Fabric Tactile Glove
hardware.taxels_note: raw channels per hand as streamed in EgoTouch (16 x 16); the release maps about 123 pressure taxels plus 15-24 finger bend sensors. JQ lists 139 sensing points for the glove in its Unitree G1 skin set.
specs: Fabric glove with a flexible fiber sensor array, signal-conditioning layer and wear-resistant outer layer (vendor)
Vendor figures: 0.01 N minimum trigger force, up to 3500 kPa (350 N/cm^2), bend radius < 0.2 mm, washable, no temperature drift
In EgoTouch: 256-channel 8-bit pressure vector per hand plus an IMU quaternion, over serial at 921600 baud; includes finger bend channels
Worn over a Rokoko Smartglove in EgoTouch
sources: https://jianyi2004.github.io/TouchAnything-Website/static/figures/data_collection.png (labels 'Outer: JQ-Industries tactile glove' / 'JQ-Industries Fabric Tactile Glove')
https://jq-industries.com/precision/glove (and the site's JS bundle, which holds the page text and specs)
unconfirmed: Maker comes from the TouchAnything project-page figure, not the paper text (paper: 'custom pressure-sensing gloves'; raw file jq_pressure.json).
Which JQ glove configuration EgoTouch used, and its native sample rate, are not stated; EgoTouch resamples everything to 30 Hz.

EgoTouch's raw streams carry signal on every channel the G1 Tactile Glove map binds (rcsv_rc_g1_tactile_glove; 137 per hand in EgoTactile's code) and use the same 921600-baud serial link; no source says whether it is the same model.
Sensing principle: JQ calls it 'flexible fiber sensing'; its foot sensor page says resistance change, the glove page does not say.
Price not published (vendor: contact sales).
year=2025: the glove is reported as part of JQ's Unitree G1 skin set in May 2025 funding news.

Image is a vendor product shot (8000x4501 PNG, about 9 MB) of a JQ-branded glove on a robot; it is the glove image the site uses for its glove product, not necessarily the exact EgoTouch configuration.
image is the page's share banner (rendered hand), not a product photo
no numeric specs on the page

hardware.name: TactiDex tactile glove (162-element)
hardware.maker: ShanghaiTech University (TactiDex authors; base glove vendor not named)
hardware.taxels_note: per glove
specs: 162 piezoresistive elements on the fingertips and palm; force resolution up to 0.01 N
Outputs raw ADC values; the authors calibrate per finger with a force gauge
Restructured by the authors to be worn over a MANUS Metagloves Pro, with a custom OptiTrack marker backplate
Left and right gloves; synchronized with 120 Hz OptiTrack/MANUS streams
unconfirmed: The paper does not name the glove's maker; it says the authors 'redesigned the structure of tactile gloves and wearing configuration', which implies an existing glove was modified. Availability 'research' reflects the modified glove; the base product may be commercial.

Same headline figures (162 elements, ~17 Hz) as the glove EgoTactile used, which EgoTactile's code identifies as JQ Industries' G1 Tactile Glove (rcsv_rc_g1_tactile_glove: 162 points, 0.01 N, 350 N max). TactiDex does not name its glove, so the entries are kept separate.
Image is a paper figure (Fig. 7) showing the tactile glove, the Metagloves Pro and the combined dual glove.

hardware.name: OpenTouch Glove
hardware.taxels_note: per hand (16 x 16 electrode grid routed into 169 taxels, palmar side)
specs: Five-layer stack: silicone / top flexible PCB electrodes / piezoresistive film (Velostat per the build docs) / bottom flexible PCB electrodes / silicone
Normal pressure only; calibrated range 0.02-50 kPa (OpenTouch paper, citing Murphy et al. CHI EA 2025)
Zero-potential scanning readout on an Adafruit Huzzah ESP32 Feather in an arm-worn enclosure; ESP-NOW wireless (USB serial, WiFi, BLE also listed), LiPo powered
Published files: readout PCB Gerbers/BOM/placement, flex-PCB Gerbers (small and large hand), laser-cut SVGs, 3D-printed enclosure STLs, design notebook for custom hand outlines; MIT License
Assembled gloves offered to academic groups through a research-kit request form (no public price)
Bench-tested to about 10k bending cycles
unconfirmed: Identity of the OpenTouch dataset glove with the 'OpenTouch Glove' build site is inferred: the OpenTouch repo README links 'Hardware' to wiresens-gloves.vercel.app, and both describe a five-layer FPC/piezoresistive stack, 16x16 readout, zero-potential circuit and ESP-NOW.
rate_hz 30 is the synchronized capture rate of the OpenTouch system; the glove's native scan rate is not stated.
Film: the paper says only 'commercial piezoresistive film'; Velostat comes from the build docs.
year 2025 from the cited design paper (Murphy et al., 'Fits like a flex-glove', CHI 2025 Extended Abstracts) and the OpenTouch preprint (Dec 2025).
Paper is ambiguous on whether fingertips/phalanges are fully covered ('uniformly cover the fingers and palmar surface'); App. D.6 says the 16x16 grid limits fingertip resolution.

hardware.name: ActionSense tactile glove
hardware.taxels_note: per hand, computed from the stated grids (23x19 palm + 5x9 thumb + 11x4 little finger + 3 x 13x4 other fingers); raw readout is a 32x32 matrix
specs: 32 conductive threads per direction taped on opposite sides of a pressure-sensitive material; each thread crossing is one sensing point
Grids: 23x19 palm, 5x9 thumb, 11x4 little finger, 13x4 each other finger
Built on open-finger gloves, so fingertips are not covered
Microcontroller and custom PCB for multiplexing and sampling, worn on the hand or arm; USB or wireless streaming
Raw ADC readings; calibration routines by pressing on a Dymo M25 postal scale and holding 5 objects
unconfirmed: Image is the project's full-body wearable-sensor photo; the tactile gloves are visible on both hands (worn together with the Manus gloves) but small. No close-up of the tactile glove was found.
rate_hz 6 is the typical achieved rate in the supplement ('improveable to ~15'); the paper's sensor table lists 15 Hz.
taxels 682 computed from the stated grids; the paper gives no total.

Construction is the same thread-crossing piezoresistive principle as STAG, but the paper cites the MIT 'intelligent carpet' (Luo et al. CVPR 2021) as prior work, not STAG; the pressure-sensitive material is not named.
Maker attribution to the Matusik lab is from the author list (DelPreto, Matusik, Rus, Torralba et al.).

hardware.name: STAG (scalable tactile glove)
hardware.taxels_note: per glove (64 electrodes, 32x32 readout, 548 valid crossings)
specs: Force-sensitive film (3M Velostat, 0.1 mm) addressed by orthogonal stainless-steel conductive threads (0.34 mm) on each side, laminated with adhesive and LDPE film onto a custom knit glove
Normal force, working range 30 mN to 0.5 N per element (responds from ~25 mN, saturates above ~0.8 N)
Electrical-grounding-based passive-matrix readout: 32 SPDT switches, 32:1 analog switch, Arduino Nano; 10-bit values
Sensor array materials about US$10; readout circuit about US$100 (paper)
Readout PCB schematic and Gerber files published on the project page; glove pattern available from the corresponding author
unconfirmed: Image is an MIT News rendering of the glove (the paper's Fig. 1 glove is also a rendering); no clean photo of the physical glove was found.

availability 'research': only the readout PCB schematic/Gerbers and the Methods description are public; the sensor sleeve pattern is 'available from the corresponding author', so it was not counted as open_hardware.

hardware.name: Knitted tactile glove (tactile textiles)
hardware.taxels_note: per glove (722 sensors over 160 cm2)
specs: Coaxial piezoresistive fibres (stainless-steel thread core, piezoresistive nanocomposite coating) inlaid orthogonally into a machine-knitted glove; each crossing is a sensor
Single sensor about 8 kOhm to 2 kOhm over 0.1-2 N; knit configurations reach 1.75 kPa sensitivity and up to 87.5 kPa range
Modified electrical-grounding-based passive-matrix readout (32x32), PCB worn on the arm
Calibrated with a self-supervised network against a digital scale (108,305 paired glove frames)
Fibre cost about US$0.2 per metre (paper)
unconfirmed: Image is the paper's Fig. 1 composite; the glove is panel b(ii) (yellow knitted glove), next to the vest, sock and robot-arm sleeve. No standalone glove photo was found.
rate ~14 Hz is stated for the whole dataset (all wearables), not specifically for the glove.
Arduino Nano readout is from the catalog's dataset entry (supplement), not re-read here.

hardware.name: VTDexManip tactile glove
hardware.taxels_note: per glove (20 discrete thin-film pressure sensors)
specs: 20 commercial thin-film piezoresistive pressure sensors: 18.3 mm diameter on the thumb tip and palm (20 g-6 kg), 10 mm elsewhere (20 g-2 kg)
Resistance-to-voltage conversion module (RKXS4040), AD7606 ADC module, STM32F205RBT6 microcontroller; serial link to a PC at 200 Hz
Each sensor calibrated against an F/T sensor at 0.5-7.5 N; trimmers set so all sensors give the same voltage for the same force; fitted curve U = 0.7216 F^0.5025 + 0.0398
Left- and right-hand gloves; worn under an outer green glove during capture with a HoloLens 2
unconfirmed: Image is the paper's dataset figure (Fig. 1); the glove photo is in panel (a), small, beside the HoloLens 2 and the outer green glove.
Coverage includes phalanges based on the sensor-position diagrams in Fig. 1(e) (dots on finger segments); the text only names thumb tip and palm for the large sensors.
Sensor vendor not named (only 'thin film pressure sensor'); the setup follows the group's earlier work (Liu et al. 2024).

hardware.name: TACROSS tactile glove
hardware.maker: The University of Hong Kong / INFIFORCE
hardware.taxels_note: per glove: 285 physical sensing locations (12x15 palm + five 3x7 finger arrays); 256 values streamed per frame
specs: Five-layer fabric stack: jersey fabric / Cu-Ni fabric electrodes / pressure-sensitive fabric / Cu-Ni fabric electrodes / jersey fabric
12-bit ADC; serial or BLE output, about 150 Hz; ~200 cm2 sensing area, >85% palmar coverage
0-20 N per taxel in the force test; repeatability 1.38% F.S., hysteresis 11.65% F.S.
Glove component BOM US$10.86 (project page); Vision-IK Ego capture rig US$520, Rokoko Ego rig US$2,150
Hardware v1 release (BOM, PCB Gerbers, pick-and-place) on GitHub, 2026-10-15; software and dataset announced
unconfirmed: Image is paper Fig. 2 (taxel map and exploded five-layer fabric stack, partly rendered); the only photo of the worn glove (assets/human-capture-original.png) shows it small on a subject.
Hardware release contains PCB/BOM files only; whether fabric-layer patterns are included was not checked (archive not opened).
No evidence found that INFIFORCE (a Chinese embodied-AI company listed as an author affiliation) sells the glove.
region 'CN' covers Hong Kong (HKU) and INFIFORCE; the schema has no separate HK value.
Paper Fig. 3 caption says '256 channels (180 palm + 105 finger sensors)', which sums to 285; the catalog counts 285 physical locations.

hardware.name: OSMO tactile glove
hardware.taxels_note: per glove: 12 three-axis taxels (5 fingertips + 7 on the palm in three sections)
hardware.price: DIY parts from WowRobo: USD 100 (magnetic skins), USD 700 (MCU board + 12 sensor boards), USD 780 (both); not a complete kit
specs: Soft magnetic elastomer over each sensor PCB with two Bosch BMM350 3-axis magnetometers (differential) and a Bosch BHI360 6-axis IMU; MuMetal shield against crosstalk
Measures normal and shear force, sensing range 0.3-80 N; raw magnetic flux (uT) used as tactile data
12 sensor PCBs on I2C to an STM32 MCU; USB-C power and data, optional LiPo + microSD for wireless use; Python and ROS2 interfaces
Intermediate and proximal phalanges left uncovered; beige outer glove for compatibility with vision hand trackers; fits a Psyonic Ability Hand
Published: BOM, sensor and glove assembly guides, PCB designs (sensor and MCU boards), firmware
unconfirmed: Sensor sample rate not stated; 25 Hz is the ROS2 logging and policy input rate in the paper.
WowRobo listing (published 2026-09-14) says lead time 3-4 weeks and that the packages are not complete glove kits; the OSMO project page links it as 'Buy DIY Kit'.
GitHub API reports no license file for the repository; the paper says complete hardware designs, firmware and assembly instructions are released.
Image is the project page's taxel-location figure (photo of the glove with sensor positions overlaid on the left half).

hardware.name: Grip System (sensor 4256E)
hardware.taxels_note: sensels per 4256E hand sensor (one hand)
specs: Thin-film pressure-mapping sensor 4256E: 18 individually positionable regions over the fingers and palm, 361 sensels, 0.158 in (4.0 mm) pitch, 0.004 in thick.
Rows and columns of conductive material with a pressure-sensitive layer at each crossing; sensel resistance falls with load.
Scan rate up to 750 Hz with the tethered VersaTek cuff/hub over USB; wireless and datalogger units also offered.
One size fits all; measures both hands simultaneously; software reports total force, peak pressure, centre of force.
ADL-21 sewed it on a cotton glove and recorded at 50 Hz with a 75 psi (517 kPa) calibration.
unconfirmed: Tekscan describes the sensing as a resistive pressure-sensitive layer at row/column crossings; 'piezoresistive' is the catalog class, not Tekscan's wording.
The 4256E page lists max pressure as '50' with no unit; the 75 psi figure is from the ADL-21 paper.
No price is published (store and quote links only); first release year not found.

hardware.name: Tactile dataglove (fabric-based sensors)
hardware.taxels_note: per hand, version used in Reach&Grasp (the 2012 paper describes 54 cells)
specs: Stretchable fabric-based piezoresistive sensor pads on the palm and the inside of the fingers; resistance read through a pull-up resistor and ADC, streamed over USB/ROS.
Reach&Grasp version: 58 taxels, 17 palm taxels in three groups, index and little finger 9 each, middle and ring 8, thumb 7; sampled at 100 Hz.
Original paper: 54 tactile cells; force range from below 0.1 N to above 30 N.
Uncalibrated in Reach&Grasp (raw values only); taxels 9, 11, 14 at the ring fingertip faulty.
Built in the EU WearHap project (grant 601165); the same glove carried CyberGlove I bend sensors for joint angles.
sources: https://pub.uni-bielefeld.de/record/2511391 (abstract via search snippet; page itself blocked by Anubis)
unconfirmed: Image is Fig. 2 of the Reach&Grasp paper (taxel map, palm view, back view with electronics), not a product photo.

The 54-cell count and 0.1-30 N range come from the Humanoids 2012 abstract as returned by search; the full paper was not read. The Reach&Grasp glove has 58 taxels, so it is a later revision or a different layout.
Reach&Grasp says one sensorized glove gave both the kinematic (CyberGlove I) and tactile data; whether Bielefeld built the tactile layer onto a CyberGlove I is inferred from that wording.
Year 2012 is the first paper; the Reach&Grasp unit was lent by Bielefeld through the NeuTouch project.

hardware.name: FSR 400 series
hardware.taxels_note: single-zone sensor; the VICON glove uses 8
specs: Single-zone force sensing resistor: polymer thick film whose resistance falls as force rises.
FSR 400: 5.08 mm diameter active area, 0.30 mm nominal thickness.
Actuation about 0.2 N, sensitivity range about 0.2-20 N; repeatability +/-2% single part, +/-6% part to part; hysteresis +10%.
Seven models in the series (400, 400 Short, 402, 402 Short, 404, 406, 408) with four connection options.
VICON glove: 8 FSRs (fingertips, thenar, distal palm), sampled at 200 Hz, individually calibrated to 61 N.
unconfirmed: VICON cites the 'FSR 400 series' datasheet; which model of the series (400, 402, ...) was used is not stated.
Product page says actuation 'as low as 0.1N', the datasheet says ~0.2 N; datasheet value used.
Sold through Interlink's online shop; no price visible on the page. Rate is set by the readout electronics, so rate_hz is null.
'Piezoresistive' is the catalog class; Interlink calls it a force sensing resistor (PTF).

hardware.name: Metagloves Pro
hardware.taxels_note: hand-tracking glove, no tactile sensing
specs: Electromagnetic-field (EMF) finger tracking: 5 fingertip EMF sensors with 6-DoF tracking each; hand module gives 3-axis wrist rotation.
Full anatomical hand model, 25 DoF; 120 Hz; latency 30 ms wired / 50 ms wireless.
USB-C or Bluetooth 5.0 dongle (up to 15 m); swappable battery, up to 3 h.
Mounting system for external trackers plus optical-marker openings in the textile; 167 g (M, with battery); sizes XS-L.
unconfirmed: TactiDex describes its mocap glove as 'IMU measurements fused with optical tracking'; MANUS specifies EMF fingertip tracking and does not name IMUs.
T-Rex: the paper says only 'Manus gloves'; the model 'Manus MetaGloves Pro' comes from the repo's hardware_code/README.md.
Year 2024 from the MANUS About page product timeline.

hardware.name: Quantum Metagloves
hardware.taxels_note: hand-tracking glove, no tactile sensing
specs: Fingertip end-point tracking sensors, 'absolute position, 3 axis rotation', millimetre accuracy.
120 Hz; signal latency <= 7.5 ms.
Bluetooth LE 5 (up to 15 m) or USB-C; swappable battery, up to 3 h.
MANUS lists it as end-of-life, no longer in production; supported through warranty.
unconfirmed: MANUS's Quantum page does not name the tracking principle; DexViTac calls the gloves 'equipped with IMUs', and the catalog's dataset entry files them as magnetic.
Year 2022 from the MANUS About page timeline.

hardware.name: Prime II Xsens
hardware.taxels_note: hand-tracking glove, no tactile sensing
specs: Finger bend (flex) sensors fused with IMUs; streams finger data directly into Xsens MVN alongside the Xsens body suit.
Xsens-glove spec sheet cited by ActionSense: 5 x 2-DoF flexible sensors and 6 x 9-DoF IMUs, 90 Hz, latency < 5 ms, proprietary 2.4 GHz wireless, 5 h swappable battery.
Open-finger textile glove; electronics module removable for washing.
ActionSense recorded it at 60 Hz and disabled the IMUs in some sessions (finger curl only, no spread).
unconfirmed: The sensor counts, 90 Hz and < 5 ms come from MANUS's 2022 'Xsens Gloves' page (the page ActionSense cites as ref. [22]); that page does not name the glove generation, and Movella lists identical numbers for the later Prime 3 Xsens.
Price USD 4,499 is the June 2020 launch price reported by Mogura VR (press), not a MANUS page.
Discontinued: MANUS moved Prime II under 'legacy products' by Sept 2021 (archived page).
Image is from MANUS's 2021 site (an Xsens-variant glove on a subject in an Xsens suit); that it shows the Prime II Xsens rather than another generation is inferred from the page date.

hardware.name: Smartgloves
hardware.taxels_note: hand-tracking glove, no tactile sensing
specs: 7 sensors per glove using hybrid IMU + EMF sensor fusion; optional Coil Pro adds absolute (drift-free) finger position.
100 fps real-time capture; WiFi streaming; swappable batteries.
Pairs with the Smartsuit Pro for synchronized full-body capture; sizes S-XL.
Succeeded by Smartgloves II (7 sensors, 250 Hz internal IMU sampling, TCP WiFi streaming).
unconfirmed: Specs and price from the December 2024 archived product page; the live page now sells Smartgloves II, and whether the first version is still sold is not stated.
Which generation each dataset used is not stated; OpenTouch's description (IMU + EMF, seven sensors per glove) matches the first version. TACROSS names only a 'Rokoko' glove.
First release year not found.

hardware.name: CyberGlove (wired, 'CyberGlove I')
hardware.taxels_note: hand-tracking glove (joint angles), no tactile sensing
specs: Resistive bend-sensing data glove, 18 or 22 joint-angle sensors (22-sensor: three flexion sensors per finger, four abduction, palm arch, wrist flexion and abduction).
Resolution < 1 deg, repeatability 3 deg between wearings, max 0.6% nonlinearity.
90 records/s typical; RS-232 (115.2 kbaud) interface unit with 25 ft cable.
Reach&Grasp used it unmodified at 100 Hz for MCP/PIP, thumb, abduction and wrist pitch/yaw.
unconfirmed: Reach&Grasp writes 'CyberGlove I'; the vendor never used that name. Specs are from the 2009 brochure for the wired CyberGlove, which is taken to be that model.
'Discontinued' is inferred: the vendor site (last updated 2017) lists only CyberGlove II/III and CyberTouch; no current page for the wired original.
The photo is the vendor's image of a CyberGlove II (its wrist unit is labelled CyberGlove II); no clean photo of the wired original was found.
In Reach&Grasp the same physical glove also carried the Bielefeld tactile sensors.
Company founding (1990) is in the brochure; the first year of this product is not stated.

hardware.name: TactileGlove II
hardware.taxels_note: per glove; elements 5.0 x 6.0 mm
specs: 65 capacitive pressure elements per glove over fingers and palm; calibrated in pressure units, force from element area
Full scale 80 psi (55 N/cm2); max force 70 N thumb/finger tips, 28 N pinky tip; minimum sensitivity 0.04 N
Scan rate 100 Hz for one glove, 50 Hz for a pair; Bluetooth 5, >2 h battery
About 2.6 mm thick; sizes S/M/M-L/L; sold as a pair or single; Chameleon 2026 software
unconfirmed: year 2020 is the launch of the original TactileGlove (PPS timeline); the release year of the II revision is not stated
PPS was founded in the US (1996); the current site footer lists only the UK office in Glasgow
coverage read from the vendor description 'fingers and palm'; exact element layout not given

hardware.name: FingerTPS II
hardware.taxels_note: one sensor per fingertip; a system ships with 2 sensors (any finger or palm)
specs: Wearable capacitive fingertip pressure sensors wired to a wrist BLE module
Force range 2 kg (4.4 lb) per sensor; accuracy error <5%; SNR 500:1; sensor 1.5 mm thick
Scan rate 25-40 Hz; Bluetooth Low Energy, 5 m range; >2 h battery
Two wrist assemblies can be used at once for bimanual tasks; calibration load cell included
unconfirmed: whether each fingertip sensor is a single element or a small array is not stated
a palm sensor option is listed but not counted in coverage

hardware.name: Tacta Glove
specs: Skill-capture glove worn by workers; uses the same tactile sensors as the Tacta Hand robot hand
Vendor says the Tacta Sensor measures force, texture and temperature
Part of a system with Tacta Hand and TactaBot; no glove specifications published
unconfirmed: image is a video poster frame from the vendor homepage showing a gloved hand; not labelled as the glove
not offered for sale on the site; availability treated as announced

hardware.name: FusionX V3 thin-film glove
hardware.taxels_note: per glove: five 4x4 patches, one per finger; no palm channels
specs: Thin-film pressure glove with five 4x4 tactile patches (80 channels, 12-bit ADC) and one bend channel per finger, plus IMU
USB serial; Python Glove SDK 0.5.0 (CPython 3.13) and FusionX GUI for Windows/Linux
GUI records gloves with a head stereo camera/IMU and optional wrist video to MCAP; GUI recording needs a TouchTronix license
Per-pixel calibration files per glove pair; earlier V1/V2 used conductive fabric
unconfirmed: region US from a third-party company profile (Buffalo, NY); no vendor website found
patch position on each finger (tip vs pad) is not stated; coverage 'tip' inferred from the per-finger layout
no product photo found; repo only has a layout diagram and GUI screenshots

hardware.name: ProGlove Gen 1
specs: Wearable sensor glove for human data capture and teleoperation of humanoid hands
Uses the same sensor skin as the company's ProHand robot hand
No sensing specifications published
unconfirmed: product page renders client-side; content taken from its meta tags plus TechCrunch (2026-06-29) and the YC launch post
whether the glove is sold separately from ProHand is not stated

hardware.name: G1 Tactile Glove
hardware.maker: JQ Industries (矩侨工业, Weihai), sold in the US by Robotics Center of Silicon Valley as the RC G1 Tactile Glove
hardware.taxels_note: per hand (fingers + palm), as listed; EgoTactile's code reads 60 fingertip and 72 palm channels plus one finger-segment channel per finger counted as six sensors
specs: 162 sensing points per hand over a 179 x 145 mm area; 4 x 6 mm sensing resolution
0.01 N recognition accuracy, max single-point pressure 350 N, repeatability +-8%
100 Hz over serial (USB), 30 Hz over Bluetooth; per-finger bend sensing; 6-axis IMU at 120 Hz
35.4 g per glove, skin <=2.33 mm; companion app exports CSV
Per Robotics Center's viewer: serial at 921600 baud, each frame 256 8-bit pressure values (16 x 16) plus an IMU quaternion
In EgoTactile: one glove on the grasping hand, read at about 17 Hz, 0-350 N range (paper)
unconfirmed: Maker: Robotics Center's viewer repo calls this the 'Juqiao G1 tactile glove'; Juqiao is the pinyin of 矩侨 (JQ Industries). JQ's own site lists no 162-point glove; it gives 139 sensing points for the glove in its Unitree G1 skin set.

EgoTactile does not name its glove. It is linked here because the channel tables in its release code (scripts/denoise.py) match the viewer's maps channel for channel and in the same order (fingertip and finger-segment channels of both hands, and the 12-channel palm row the viewer reads), and the paper's 162 sensors and 0-350 N match this listing. Co-author Yaqi Qin is listed at JQ Industries, Qingdao.

Finger segments: Robotics Center lists per-finger bend sensing, and its viewer reads channels 35-47 (right glove) and 210-222 (left) as finger bend. EgoTactile's code names the same channels BENDS, while its paper treats each as the mean of a six-sensor pressure group on the finger's middle and proximal segments.
EgoTactile read the glove at about 17 Hz, below the listed 100 Hz serial rate; the paper does not say how it was connected.
the only product image the store serves is 128 px wide
coverage from 'fingers + palm'

hardware.name: pliance glove system
hardware.taxels_note: configurable: 5-12 finger sensors plus a 64-element palm matrix
specs: Elastic capacitive sensor matrices worn on the hand; each element individually calibrated (trublu air-pressure calibrator)
Five to twelve finger sensors and one 64-element palm sensor; about two sensors per cm2
Typically 20 Hz, higher when fewer sensors are active; pliance analyser handles up to 1,024 sensors
Fibre optic/USB or Bluetooth to a Windows PC; sync with video, EMG and motion capture
unconfirmed: total taxel count depends on the sensor configuration and is not given as one number

hardware.name: loadglove
hardware.taxels_note: 1 palm loadpad + 1-13 finger buttonsens, each a total-force sensor
specs: Calibrated textile capacitive force sensors: one loadpad (90 x 80 mm, 10-4000 N) and 1-13 buttonsens (17 x 17 mm, 2.5-60 N or 10-150 N)
Total normal force per sensor, no spatial resolution within a sensor; accuracy +-10%
